scope: authored source-linked observations, with measurement gates left unresolved

observations.context: Wells and reconstructed built-up extent
observations.dating_basis: Urban-context attribution; no annual service chronology
observations.source_observation: An estimate of 700 wells applies an average catchment spacing to the inferred built-up area, including unexcavated sectors.
observations.author_interpretation: City-scale water provision extrapolation.
observations.renewal_question: A possible starting-asset inventory requires actual counts and coverage.
observations.inference_limits: The 700 estimate is not a recovered stock or a bound on delivered usable water.
alternative_explanations: Unexcavated areas differ in well density
observations.evidence_lineage: Mohenjo-Daro legacy excavations and Jansen reanalysis

observations.context: Street drains, settling pits and house effluent disposal
observations.dating_basis: Architectural context; cleaning cycles undated
observations.source_observation: Drain covers were removable; settling pits had access steps. Catchment vessels and soak pits provided other local disposal routes.
observations.author_interpretation: The design could allow cleaning and sediment removal.
observations.renewal_question: Define maintenance access and service substitutes before assuming a single network route.
observations.inference_limits: Access geometry alone does not count performed cleanings or identify their organizers.
alternative_explanations: Some accessible installations were seldom cleaned
observations.evidence_lineage: Mohenjo-Daro legacy excavations and Jansen reanalysis

observations.context: Deep excavation, southern DK-G sector
observations.dating_basis: Vertical section relationships; city-wide height equivalence rejected
observations.source_observation: Three successive drain rebuilding phases are reported at differing elevations within this sector.
observations.author_interpretation: Linked drain units may improve local relative chronology.
observations.renewal_question: Repeated rebuilding supplies direct renewal candidates.
observations.inference_limits: Relative phases do not measure interval lengths, joint deadlines or uninterrupted service.
alternative_explanations: Later buildings connect to older drains
observations.evidence_lineage: Mohenjo-Daro legacy excavations and Jansen reanalysis

observations.locus: Printed p.66 / composite PDF p.24, Flow capacity estimates
observations.context: Legacy drain network reconstruction
observations.dating_basis: Legacy level label; not accepted as a unified stratigraphic phase
observations.source_observation: A 1977 attempt could not calculate complete interconnected-network flow because no intact network was available.
observations.author_interpretation: Mixed versus separated effluent could not be resolved by that calculation.
observations.renewal_question: Actual delivered drainage cannot be supplied by the preserved widths alone.
observations.inference_limits: Neither complete network capacity nor required municipal workload follows from this record.
observations.evidence_lineage: Mohenjo-Daro legacy excavations and Jansen reanalysis

observations.context: Southern DK-G drain links and published plans
observations.dating_basis: Hypothesized broad cofunction; vertical profiles where available
observations.source_observation: Interconnecting drains are proposed as evidence for broad contemporaneity of served buildings, while elevation-based city-wide chronology is questioned.
observations.author_interpretation: Reconstruct local operational networks from relationships and field records.
observations.renewal_question: A shared interface can identify which repair tasks could concern the same functional cluster.
observations.inference_limits: The functional association must be checked; height and a connected line do not establish simultaneous repairs.
alternative_explanations: Reused drain serves a later building
Visible segments belonged to separate episodes
observations.evidence_lineage: Mohenjo-Daro legacy excavations and Jansen reanalysis

observations.context: Mound E perimeter wall
observations.dating_basis: Paper's phase ranges and stratigraphic associations; 3A starts 2600/2550, 3C ends 2000/1900
observations.source_observation: The wall was rebuilt at least once and repaired several times; major work is associated tentatively with Periods 3B and 3C.
observations.author_interpretation: Continued wall importance within changing urban organization.
observations.renewal_question: Replacement and repair are observed separately from original construction.
observations.inference_limits: Phase ranges are uncertain and too broad for annual resource requirements.
alternative_explanations: Repair episodes spread across decades or centuries
observations.evidence_lineage: Harappa Archaeological Research Project, Mound E excavations

observations.context: Mound E gateway, western earlier drains and later eastern culvert
observations.phase: Earlier successive drains; last assigned Period 3C
observations.dating_basis: Local stratigraphic ordering and source phase attribution
observations.source_observation: Three earlier drains were recorded; the last was corbelled and clogged with silty refuse. After it ceased functioning, a new culvert was dug farther east through the former gateway.
observations.author_interpretation: Drain replacement changed the passage's use.
observations.renewal_question: This is the first pilot for reconstructing an actual renewal operation and substitute route.
observations.inference_limits: The sequence does not give the downtime, sediment accumulation rate, throughput, labor duration or responsible institution.
alternative_explanations: Refuse entered during abandonment rather than causing failure
The new route served changed demand
A functional alternative operated during the gap
observations.evidence_lineage: Harappa Archaeological Research Project, Mound E excavations

observations.context: Gateway circulation and street levels
observations.dating_basis: Architecture and street associations
observations.source_observation: A later corbelled culvert partly obstructed an older doorway; streets and alternative side passages were modified.
observations.author_interpretation: Access and drainage changed together.
observations.renewal_question: Test obligations at interfaces where one service can obstruct another.
observations.inference_limits: The observed layout does not establish a municipal decision procedure or simultaneous work dates.
alternative_explanations: Traffic demand shifted before drain construction
observations.evidence_lineage: Harappa Archaeological Research Project, Mound E excavations

observations.context: Stage III city walls and subsequent extensions
observations.dating_basis: Structural stage ordering; cause is excavator interpretation
observations.source_observation: Large repairs and extensions are reported after extensive structural damage within Stage III.
observations.author_interpretation: Excavators identify a catastrophic earthquake.
observations.renewal_question: Disturbance-specific repair is a candidate; the hazard attribution needs independent assessment.
observations.inference_limits: Neither earthquake timing nor a shared emergency work budget is measured here.
observations.evidence_lineage: ASI Dholavira excavation programme

observations.context: Outer walls supporting some reservoirs
observations.phase: Stage VI after a brief desertion
observations.dating_basis: Reported local stratigraphic stages with an explicit interruption
observations.source_observation: After desertion, later occupants retained wall segments important to some reservoirs.
observations.author_interpretation: Useful inherited water structures remained part of a changed settlement.
observations.renewal_question: Selective retention allows a service-specific persistence test after an occupation break.
observations.inference_limits: This is not an uninterrupted city or a measurement of reservoir output.
observations.outcome_unit: selected reservoir-support wall segments and later settlement
observations.evidence_lineage: ASI Dholavira excavation programme

observations.context: Later houses, streets and older structures
observations.dating_basis: Local stage relationships
observations.source_observation: Stone was taken from earlier structures for houses, while new streets, alleys and housing sectors replaced the earlier arrangement.
observations.author_interpretation: Material reuse accompanied transformed settlement organization.
observations.renewal_question: Salvage could reduce new material requirements while preserving shelter.
observations.inference_limits: The report does not quantify salvaged volume, labor savings, resident continuity or ownership rules.
observations.evidence_lineage: ASI Dholavira excavation programme

observations.context: East reservoir, northern embankment
observations.dating_basis: Local construction and repair relationships; Chapter 5 broad reconstruction
observations.source_observation: A damaged embankment was repaired with sticky clay, stone fragments and pottery over underlying sand and clay.
observations.author_interpretation: A major collapse was repaired; reservoir form is mainly attributed to Stage IV.
observations.renewal_question: Local materials and retained geometry define a specific water-storage repair candidate.
observations.inference_limits: Construction traces do not give timing within the phase or repair productivity.
alternative_explanations: Material belongs to an altered bank rather than a like-for-like repair
observations.evidence_lineage: ASI Dholavira excavation programme

observations.context: East reservoir descent and bedrock
observations.dating_basis: Wear and added access blocks; exact episode not dated
observations.source_observation: Worn rock and steps are associated with added stone blocks near the lowest step.
observations.author_interpretation: Excavators infer repeated water-fetching and modified descent access.
observations.renewal_question: Maintaining access is a separate task from maintaining the reservoir bank.
observations.inference_limits: Groundwater supply and year-round drought operation are suggested, not established by the wear alone.
alternative_explanations: Changes in water level or access route
observations.evidence_lineage: ASI Dholavira excavation programme

observations.context: East reservoir fill and later surfaces
observations.phase: Stage V damage; later V and VI activity
observations.dating_basis: Report's broad stage reconstruction and fill/activity relationships
observations.source_observation: Collapsed bank debris and sediment filled much of the reservoir; fireplaces and kilns appeared on later surfaces. The excavator reports cessation of water function.
observations.author_interpretation: Damage is attributed to gushing floodwater; the later activity may have included occasional gatherings.
observations.renewal_question: Activity at the same locus can persist after the water service ends.
observations.inference_limits: Printed p.164 explicitly excludes regular continuous occupation in this area. Extending the failure to all eastern reservoirs and attributing it to poverty are inferences.
alternative_explanations: Alternative water sources or smaller demand
Repair infeasible under changed physical conditions
observations.outcome_unit: one excavated reservoir's function and later episodic activity
observations.evidence_lineage: ASI Dholavira excavation programme

observations.context: Broad stages, interruptions and chronology table
observations.dating_basis: Stratigraphic and typological sequence with limited, partly inconsistent TL checks
observations.source_observation: The report reconstructs seven stages over a long interval, including a desertion before VI and a longer uncertain break before VII.
observations.author_interpretation: Stage VI is described as a smaller transformed town; VII uses a changed house form.
observations.renewal_question: Define reoccupation and configuration change explicitly when describing long duration.
observations.inference_limits: The table is not evidence for continuous occupation, stable population or annual service schedules.
alternative_explanations: Different zones occupied at different times
Hiatus length differs from the reconstruction
observations.evidence_lineage: ASI Dholavira excavation programme

observations.locus: Publisher XML §§Sec9, Sec10, Sec13, Sec16–Sec17 and Table 4
observations.site: LWS northwest India sites and reviewed Indus assemblages
observations.context: Crop and weed assemblages by site and phase
observations.phase: Early, Mature, Late Harappan; selected later contexts
observations.dating_basis: Context and phase assignments from constituent excavations; botanical and weed ecology
observations.source_observation: Assemblages vary by site and phase; combined crops, weeds and ecological expectations are used to reconstruct different seasonal management strategies.
observations.author_interpretation: Indus cultivation followed several locally adapted strategies.
observations.renewal_question: Potential supply alternatives need their actual growing conditions and seasonal requirements specified.
observations.inference_limits: Crop presence does not quantify food delivered or failure covariance across seasons.
alternative_explanations: Purchased or stored crops enter an assemblage
observations.outcome_unit: site-phase botanical samples and proposed cultivation
observations.evidence_lineage: Land, Water and Settlement archaeobotany plus previously published site assemblages

observations.context: Plant-remain interpretation
observations.dating_basis: Definitions and archaeological sampling processes
observations.source_observation: Growing multiple crops on the same parcel differs from finding seasonal crops in a settlement. Postharvest and postdepositional mixing can obscure field practice.
observations.author_interpretation: Crop and weed ecology plus other methods can refine practice reconstruction.
observations.renewal_question: Avoid counting crop names as independent productive options.
observations.inference_limits: Species diversity alone cannot establish sequential use of the same land or a resilience coefficient.
observations.evidence_lineage: Land, Water and Settlement archaeobotany plus previously published site assemblages

observations.site: Masudpur I, Masudpur VII and LWS region
observations.context: Village agriculture, pottery and urban connections
observations.phase: Before, during and after urban occupation
observations.dating_basis: Source contexts and broad phases; uneven chronological precision
observations.source_observation: Multi-season crop use and village material diversity predate the end of urbanism; rural sites combine local ceramic traditions with other objects connecting them to wider networks.
observations.author_interpretation: Local flexibility and regional variation may have supported changing settlement forms.
observations.renewal_question: Renewal options can exist before a disturbance; posturban change need not be a new invention.
observations.inference_limits: The crop data overlap S06. They do not establish continuity of individual households or a response dated to a specific climate year.
alternative_explanations: Trade links change while cultivation persists
observations.outcome_unit: sampled rural practices and regional connections
observations.evidence_lineage: Land, Water and Settlement environmental, village and regional research

observations.context: Water sources and settlement setting
observations.dating_basis: Environmental observations plus reconstructed availability
observations.source_observation: Rainfall, runoff, overbank water, wells and ponds offer different possible supplies; large canals are not established for the study area.
observations.author_interpretation: Locally different water access could support different cultivation strategies.
observations.renewal_question: Map upstream and seasonal dependencies rather than assuming all water routes are independent.
observations.inference_limits: The source does not quantify each route's output or reliability for each settlement.
alternative_explanations: Small water-control techniques leave little trace
Water source access changes between phases
observations.evidence_lineage: Land, Water and Settlement environmental, village and regional research

observations.context: Lapidary drill roughouts, waste and grinding traces
observations.dating_basis: Production contexts, wear and experimental reconstruction
observations.source_observation: Roughouts and microdebitage support a multistage process for making specialized drills; tang wear also supports reuse of exhausted drills as pivots.
observations.author_interpretation: Tools supporting bead manufacture were themselves produced and recycled.
observations.renewal_question: A craft's renewal network includes replacement tools, not only bead stock or finished bead makers.
observations.inference_limits: The reconstructed sequence does not measure ancient throughput or practitioner succession.
alternative_explanations: Some drill blanks arrived from elsewhere
Different steps occurred in different workshops
observations.evidence_lineage: Indus lapidary finds at Mohenjo-Daro, Harappa and Chanhu-Daro plus modern drilling experiments

observations.context: Specialized drill morphology and wear
observations.dating_basis: Wear and morphology; reconstructed mechanics
observations.source_observation: Repeated grinding renewed cutting edges, reduced drill dimensions and could permit exhausted long drills to serve smaller beads.
observations.author_interpretation: Resharpening prolonged useful tool operation.
observations.renewal_question: Repair, downsizing and material substitution can provide different renewal routes.
observations.inference_limits: The number of cycles and cumulative ancient usable output are not known.
alternative_explanations: Breakage ended a tool before repeated reuse
observations.evidence_lineage: Indus lapidary finds at Mohenjo-Daro, Harappa and Chanhu-Daro plus modern drilling experiments

observations.context: One experimenter's bead drilling
observations.dating_basis: Reported experiment dates, not ancient dates
observations.source_observation: With Kenoyer as operator, five specialized-stone trials averaged 2.37 mm/hour; the reported green-jasper comparison was 0.83 mm/hour. Other tools and experienced modern operators yielded different rates.
observations.author_interpretation: Tool properties and operator experience affect drilling performance.
observations.renewal_question: A replacement input's usefulness must be measured, not inferred from similar appearance.
observations.inference_limits: Experimental hours are not ancient labor coefficients; operators, tools, specimen properties and experience differ across comparisons.
observations.evidence_lineage: Indus lapidary finds at Mohenjo-Daro, Harappa and Chanhu-Daro plus modern drilling experiments

observations.context: Inferred technical learning
observations.dating_basis: Technological interpretation
observations.source_observation: The authors propose closely supervised apprenticeship for specialized drill manufacture and use.
observations.author_interpretation: Complex technique may have required protected skill transmission.
observations.renewal_question: Test skill renewal separately from tool presence and stylistic repetition.
observations.inference_limits: The article observes neither ancient apprentices nor the duration, organization or exclusivity of instruction.
observations.evidence_lineage: Indus lapidary finds at Mohenjo-Daro, Harappa and Chanhu-Daro plus modern drilling experiments

observations.site: Indus craft and modern Pakistan comparison
observations.context: Local/nonlocal materials and production techniques
observations.dating_basis: Comparative framework; no uninterrupted lineage dated
observations.source_observation: The author separates material access from technical demands and discusses modern crafts using widely available clay and fuel.
observations.author_interpretation: Dispersed access and broadly learned techniques could facilitate persistence.
observations.renewal_question: Supplier access and skill availability are separate prerequisites; count them separately.
observations.inference_limits: Modern craft organization does not identify Harappan governance or prove an unbroken cultural lineage.
alternative_explanations: Learning through contact or new practitioners
observations.evidence_lineage: Kenoyer Indus craft synthesis and modern Pakistan analogy

observations.context: Specialized stone drill use after urban contraction
observations.dating_basis: Regional material-synthesis attribution; not an annual dated event
observations.observation_type: reported technology loss and competing conjectures
observations.source_observation: The synthesis reports the end of specialized drilling-stone use and changing access to distant materials.
observations.author_interpretation: A secret source, loss of knowledgeable specialists or interruption of an external source are proposed explanations.
observations.renewal_question: Distinguish a missing raw input from missing technique or declining demand.
observations.inference_limits: The stone's source and the causal reason for its loss are unresolved.
alternative_explanations: Demand for long hard-stone beads declined
observations.evidence_lineage: Kenoyer stone-bead synthesis, partly reusing Indus technological research

observations.context: Reported alternative drills and imitation materials
observations.dating_basis: Comparative artefact/technology synthesis; sites differ
observations.source_observation: The synthesis describes abrasive tubular drills for smaller beads and faience imitating more restricted valued materials.
observations.author_interpretation: Different production configurations could preserve some ornament use.
observations.renewal_question: Define the surviving function and acceptable change before classifying craft failure.
observations.inference_limits: Finished resemblance does not prove local manufacture or an apprenticeship lineage at each later site.
alternative_explanations: Changed preference rather than constrained substitution
observations.evidence_lineage: Kenoyer stone-bead synthesis, partly reusing Indus technological research

observations.context: Shell workshop, raw material stocks, drills, waste and crucibles
observations.dating_basis: Excavated context and broad occupational sequence
observations.source_observation: Shell blanks, waste and raw stock occur in a workshop; bead materials, drills and production debris occur in other areas; crucibles retain copper adhesion.
observations.author_interpretation: The site participated in several craft and exchange activities.
observations.renewal_question: Inventory the distinct production stages and their material dependencies.
observations.inference_limits: Stocks and site area do not determine population, annual output, smelting capacity or trade volume.
alternative_explanations: Stored raw material served external users
observations.evidence_lineage: Gola Dhoro excavation programme

observations.context: Discarded raw shell and sorted jasper stock
observations.dating_basis: Material observations with preliminary source distances
observations.source_observation: Poor shell material was discarded after arrival, and sorted jasper stock lacked matching manufacturing waste in some areas.
observations.author_interpretation: The authors propose separate shell collectors and distribution of some stock rather than all on-site processing.
observations.renewal_question: More suppliers may still share one collector, route or material source.
observations.inference_limits: Specific collectors, deliveries and upstream monopoly are inferred, not directly counted.
alternative_explanations: Stock intended for future local work
observations.evidence_lineage: Gola Dhoro excavation programme

observations.context: Last occupation phase
observations.phase: Late occupation reported through about 1700 BCE
observations.dating_basis: Broad field-note phase attribution; no absolute-date table inspected
observations.source_observation: Occupation reportedly continued into a later phase after specialized crafts, trading activity, fort-wall use and inscribed steatite seals ended.
observations.author_interpretation: Settlement activity persisted after the earlier urban-connected production configuration changed.
observations.renewal_question: Use settlement continuation and craft/network continuation as different outcomes.
observations.inference_limits: The phase statement does not fix resident continuity, precise change dates or the cause of losses.
observations.outcome_unit: reported occupation versus named craft and network indicators
observations.evidence_lineage: Gola Dhoro excavation programme

observations.context: Selected dated or phase-attributed vessel fragments
observations.phase: Mainly Mature Harappan, selected earlier/later contexts
observations.dating_basis: Context dating and ceramic phase attribution
observations.source_observation: The sample targeted vessel fragments from selected contexts. The text gives 172 samples whereas the Table 4 site-count row sums to 171.
observations.author_interpretation: The sample measures preserved residues in those vessels.
observations.renewal_question: Keep sampling coverage explicit before comparing service or food continuity.
observations.inference_limits: Preserved pot residues are neither food mass nor a random sample of residents' meals; the source count discrepancy remains unresolved.
alternative_explanations: Sampling by vessel form and context
observations.evidence_lineage: LWS rural sites plus Farmana and Rakhigarhi ceramic-residue samples

observations.site: Rural and urban northwest India sites
observations.context: Lipid isotope comparisons across settlements and selected periods
observations.dating_basis: Uneven phase coverage and contexts; no annual panel
observations.source_observation: The authors report broad similarities in residue signatures and no detected period effect in their cross-period comparison, with limited samples.
observations.author_interpretation: Some rural culinary practices may have continued during wider urban changes.
observations.renewal_question: Daily practice can be compared separately from urban form or a trade network.
observations.inference_limits: Non-detection is not an equivalence result or proof of stable whole diets, resident identity or adequate provisioning.
alternative_explanations: Broad isotope classes mask changing ingredients
Mixtures and small samples obscure change
observations.outcome_unit: measured residue signatures in selected vessels
observations.evidence_lineage: LWS rural sites plus Farmana and Rakhigarhi ceramic-residue samples

observations.context: C3/C4 food webs, vessel mixtures and reference baselines
observations.dating_basis: Biomolecular interpretation
observations.source_observation: Several food sources and mixtures can produce overlapping isotope signatures; the authors request regional reference fats and broader well-dated sampling.
observations.author_interpretation: Residue classes retain ambiguity about specific ingredients.
observations.renewal_question: Continuity tests require an outcome marker capable of distinguishing the proposed change.
observations.inference_limits: A coarse unchanged signature cannot identify identical recipes or food quantities.
observations.evidence_lineage: LWS rural sites plus Farmana and Rakhigarhi ceramic-residue samples

observations.context: Cemetery R-37, Cemetery H stratum II and Area G
observations.phase: Urban, urban–posturban and posturban selected burials
observations.dating_basis: R-37 reported calibrated range; H phase attribution; Area G ceramic-relative placement without absolute dates
observations.source_observation: The analytic sample is 115 individuals after 45 of the 160 examined were excluded. Disease indicators differ between burial groups and periods.
observations.author_interpretation: The authors relate some differences to social vulnerability and changing conditions.
observations.renewal_question: Long occupation should not be treated as equivalent to equal access or healthy persistence for all residents.
observations.inference_limits: Funerary inclusion, preservation and excavation select the sample; group differences do not estimate living-population prevalence or alone identify political organization.
observations.evidence_lineage: Harappa skeletal collections excavated in 1923–1967

observations.context: Compiled sites and survey coverage
observations.phase: Early, Mature, Late Harappan and later broad periods
observations.dating_basis: Site report phase assignments, uneven field survey coverage and location precision
observations.source_observation: The compilation suggests agglomeration and later redistribution, while northeastern reoccupation and missing later sites may reflect older survey methods and gaps. LWS surveys did not show a universal local posturban increase.
observations.author_interpretation: New survey and revisitation could test regional reorganization.
observations.renewal_question: Regional relocation is a possible renewal route requiring its own sampling and population evidence.
observations.inference_limits: Site dots are not resident numbers, migration identities or proof that all period-assigned sites were occupied together.
observations.evidence_lineage: Northwest India multi-project settlement compilation, including LWS surveys
